line: Hi. Alan Fong. I have the pharmacy on Grand, Fong's. I'm dropping off the seniors' pill organizers.
Fourteen boxes, all labelled, every Thursday. You're new? I don't think you've been in the pharmacy.
choice1: New-ish. I need to find a pharmacy, actually.

line: Open till seven, Saturdays till two. Bring your insurance card the first time, it saves twenty minutes. Honestly, most people forget it.
choice1: Do you know everyone here, then?
choice2: Insurance card. Got it. See you.

line: Their pills, mostly. Blood pressure, cholesterol, one man who lies to me about his diet every month. I fill for half this building.
choice1: Did you grow up around here?

line: I came from Hong Kong at twelve. Grand Avenue, the high school, then pharmacy school two states away. Then I came back and bought the shop from the man who'd had it since 1970.
Ethan and Chloe? No. Chloe can order dim sum. That's the whole inheritance.
Honestly? No. My kids won't need any of this, and that's fine. Ethan's applying to engineering schools. Nobody there is going to ask if he knows his tones.
Then he'll take a class, like anybody. My mother lived her whole life with one foot in Kowloon. I spent mine getting both feet here. I'm not sorry.
Hi. Alan Fong, Fong's Pharmacy, on Grand. Dropping off insulin pens for Dr. Haddad's patients. You look like you've been waiting a while.
choice3: I'd rather not chat right now.

line: The desk is short two people today. Take a number from the red machine, not the blue one. The blue one's been broken since June.
Tuesdays and Fridays. The clinic orders, I deliver, it saves their patients a bus ride. Twelve pens today, one cooler bag.
choice1: So you know the patients too?

line: Hi. Mr. Guo wants me on the board again.
Every year he asks, every year I say the same thing. I'll fill the pill boxes. I won't sit through the meetings.
Three hours, on the budget. I did one year, 2011. I proposed we put the money into a citizenship class. Nobody spoke to me for the rest of the meeting.
choice1: What do you think the center should do?

line: Help people get on here. English classes, the citizenship test, how to read a lease. Guo wants everything the way it was in 1985. He does the lunch very well. I'll give him that.
Morning. Mrs. Chen asked me to print her labels in Chinese.
The system can. I told her she should learn 'twice a day with food.' She called me a bad boy. I'm fifty-seven.
choice3: I'll let you work it out.

line: Both languages, English on top. She can read 'with food' fine. She just likes to see the other one.
choice1: Why does it matter which is on top?

line: Honestly, because the emergency room reads the top line. If she's on the floor at two in the morning, the paramedic doesn't read Chinese. The aunties think I'm stubborn. I'm thinking about the paramedic.
choice2: Both on the label would help.

line: Hey. You have a minute? My nephew is opening his own business, and I'm about to give him advice he didn't ask for.
Put your English name on the business card. Not instead. First. People call back the name they can say.
They can. Mostly they don't. When I opened, the sign said Fong Kwok-wah Pharmacy. Six slow months. I changed it to Fong's, and the next month there was a line.
choice1: Did that feel like giving something up?

line: Honestly, a little, the first week. Then I was paying the mortgage. Kwok-wah is still on my licence. My mother still calls me that. That's enough places for it.
choice2: I'd keep it on the sign.

line: Good, you're here. Are you free Sunday?
Ethan's soccer team has a barbecue at our place. Twenty families, one grill, my wife in charge. Come. Nobody talks about the old country.
Parents from the team. A dentist, two teachers, a man who sells boats. They talk about college visits and the referee. It's very relaxing.
Hi. Sorry, it's been a strange week at the counter.
Three customers asked me this week if the pharmacy reports to immigration.
No. We report to the state board, and only about controlled drugs. I told them three times, with the form numbers.
Two did. One paid cash and didn't give her name. $ Honestly, I've been a citizen thirty years, and last night I checked my passport drawer.
choice2: You've got nothing to worry about.

line: Hi. Good news for the seniors, at least.
The state is paying for translated prescription labels now. Seven languages, it prints them for free.
It is good. For Mrs. Chen, for Mr. Lin. They're past seventy-five, they're not going to learn 'with food' now.
My worry is the young ones. A twenty-five-year-old asks me for the Chinese label and I think, you'll need English at the doctor, at the bank, at work. I don't say it. I think it.
choice1: The labels are for the seniors.
choice2: They'll learn it at work, like you did.

line: You're at the center every time I come.
Careful. Guo will have you running the committee, and then it's your whole life.
Ask Mrs. Ho. She did the books for him twenty years. Her own kids she sees at Christmas.
For her, maybe not. For you? Honestly, you're young. Use the center for what you need, the lunch, the lawyer on Saturdays. Then go do your life out there. That's what it was for when it started.
choice1: That's one way to see it.

line: I hear you're at the library, the merchants' thing, everywhere. Good.
That's how it works. Ten years, nobody asks where you're from.
You don't mind now. Wait until it's the fortieth time.
choice1: Did people ask you a lot?

line: Every day, at school, 1981. 'Where are you really from.' I said Grand Avenue until they stopped. It took three years. Now the merchants elect me treasurer and nobody asks me anything.
Alan is counting boxes and doesn't look up.
Fine. Forgotten. Thirteen, fourteen. Okay, all here.
Fourteen boxes, thirteen labels. Somebody's Tuesday pills are missing. Not now.
